# Strings {#sec-strings}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```

In R, text lives in character vectors, and a single string is a character vector of length one. Rust has no character vector. It has two string types instead: `String`, which owns its text and can grow, and `&str`, which refers to text stored somewhere else. The split is the same one @sec-vectors drew between a `Vec` and a slice. This chapter covers both types, the everyday operations on them, and the main surprise for R users, which is that Rust measures and slices strings in bytes rather than characters. The matching sections of the Rust book are "Storing UTF-8 Encoded Text with Strings" and "The Slice Type" [@rustbook, secs. 8.2, 4.3].

## Two string types

In R, a string is a character vector of length one:

```{r}
#| label: r-string
x <- "hello"
typeof(x)
length(x)
nchar(x)
```

Rust has two types, and the comments mark which is which:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-string-types
let greeting = "hello"; // a &str: text built into the program
let mut owned = String::from("hello"); // a String: text the program owns
owned.push_str(", world");
println!("{greeting}");
println!("{owned}");
```

A string literal such as `"hello"` is a `&str`. Its text is compiled into the program, and you can read it but not change it. A `String` owns its text, so with `mut` you can add to it, as `push_str()` does here. In Rust, `String::from("hello")` makes a `String` from a `&str`, and so does `"hello".to_string()`.

A `String` owns its characters the way a `Vec<i32>` owns its numbers, and a `&str` refers to text the way a slice refers to part of a vector: all of a `String`, part of one, or text built into the program.

R has only one kind of string, and it never changes. In R, `paste0(x, ", world")` builds a new string and leaves `x` alone, which is closer to Rust's `&str` than to a `String` you can grow in place.

## Strings as function arguments

A function that only reads text should take a `&str`. It then accepts a string literal and a `String` alike, just as `total()` in @sec-vectors accepts a whole vector or a slice of one:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-str-argument
fn shout(text: &str) -> String {
    text.to_uppercase()
}

fn main() {
    let owned = String::from("hello");
    println!("{}", shout("hi"));
    println!("{}", shout(&owned));
}
```

The `shout()` function returns a `String` because it creates new text. That gives a rule I'll follow in this book for functions that build new text: take `&str`, return `String`. A function that returns part of its input, as `trim()` does below, can return a `&str` instead; @sec-borrowing explains how.

## Building strings

R builds strings with `paste()`, `paste0()`, and `sprintf()`:

```{r}
#| label: r-build
name <- "Ada"
year <- 1843L
sprintf("%s wrote the first program in %d", name, year)
paste0(name, " wrote the first program in ", year)
```

Rust's `format!` takes the same template as `println!` but returns the text as a `String` instead of printing it:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-build
let name = "Ada";
let year = 1843;
let note = format!("{name} wrote the first program in {year}");
println!("{note}");
```

## Common operations

Most of R's common string functions have a Rust method that does the same job:

```{r}
#| label: r-ops
s <- "  Hello, World  "
trimws(s)
grepl("World", s, fixed = TRUE)
startsWith(trimws(s), "Hello")
gsub("World", "R", s, fixed = TRUE)
toupper(s)
```

```{rust}
#| label: rust-ops
let s = "  Hello, World  ";
println!("{}", s.trim());
println!("{}", s.contains("World"));
println!("{}", s.trim().starts_with("Hello"));
println!("{}", s.replace("World", "R"));
println!("{}", s.to_uppercase());
```

Rust's `replace()` changes every match, like `gsub()` rather than `sub()`. Methods such as `trim()` that return part of the original text give back a `&str`; methods that build new text, such as `replace()` and `to_uppercase()`, return a `String`.

The pairs agree on plain ASCII text but can differ beyond it. R's `trimws()` removes spaces, tabs, and line breaks, while Rust's `trim()` removes any Unicode whitespace, including a non-breaking space. Rust's `to_uppercase()` turns `ß` into `SS`; R's `toupper("straße")` leaves it as it is.

::: {.callout-warning title="Where the analogy breaks"}
R's `grepl()`, `sub()`, `gsub()`, and `strsplit()` treat the pattern as a regular expression unless you pass `fixed = TRUE`. Given a string as the pattern, Rust's `contains()`, `replace()`, and `split()` match it literally, and the standard library has no regular expressions at all. They come from the `regex` crate, an add-on package of the kind Part V introduces.
:::

R splits text with `strsplit()`, Rust with `split()`:

```{r}
#| label: r-split
strsplit("a,b,c", ",", fixed = TRUE)
```

```{rust}
#| label: rust-split
for part in "a,b,c".split(",") {
    println!("{part}");
}
```

R's `strsplit()` returns a list because it works on every element of a character vector at once. Rust's `split()` works on one string and hands back the pieces one at a time, so a `for` loop can walk through them. Collecting the pieces into a vector takes an iterator method that @sec-iterators covers.

The two also disagree at the end of the text: splitting `"a,b,"` gives `"a"`, `"b"`, and an empty `""` in Rust, but R's `strsplit()` drops the final empty piece.

## Vectors of strings

R's string functions are vectorized. Rust's string methods work on one string, so a vector of strings needs a loop, as in @sec-vectors:

```{r}
#| label: r-vector-strings
fruits <- c("apple", "kiwi")
toupper(fruits)
```

```{rust}
#| label: rust-vector-strings
let fruits = vec!["apple", "kiwi"];
let mut upper = Vec::new();
for fruit in fruits {
    upper.push(fruit.to_uppercase());
}
println!("{:?}", upper);
```

Here, `fruits` is a `Vec<&str>` of literals, and `upper` is a `Vec<String>` because `to_uppercase()` builds new strings. The `{:?}` form prints strings with quotes around them.

## Length is measured in bytes

Rust stores text as UTF-8, the same encoding R uses on most systems. In UTF-8, plain ASCII letters take one byte each, but a letter such as `é` takes two. R's `nchar()` counts characters by default. Rust's `len()` counts bytes [@rustbook, sec. 8.2]:

```{r}
#| label: r-nchar
nchar("café")
nchar("café", type = "bytes")
```

```{rust}
#| label: rust-len
let word = "café";
println!("{}", word.len());
println!("{}", word.chars().count());
```

To count characters in Rust, call `chars()`, which goes through the text one character at a time, and then `count()`; @sec-iterators covers methods like these.

What both languages count as a character is a Unicode scalar value, which Rust calls a `char`. That's usually what you'd expect, but a letter written with a separate combining accent, or a flag emoji, counts as two in both.

::: {.callout-tip title="The same idea in R"}
R keeps track of the same difference, through the `type` argument of `nchar()`. The two languages pick different defaults: R counts characters unless you ask for bytes, and Rust counts bytes unless you ask for characters.
:::

## Slicing strings

R's `substr()` takes character positions. A Rust `&str` is sliced with a range, like a vector in @sec-vectors. Here both take the first three characters:

```{r}
#| label: r-substr
substr("café", 1, 3)
```

```{rust}
#| label: rust-slice
let word = "café";
println!("{}", &word[0..3]);
```

The range counts bytes, not characters. Here that makes no difference, because `c`, `a`, and `f` take one byte each. A range that ends in the middle of `é` fails:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-slice-panic
#| error: true
let word = "café";
println!("{}", &word[0..4]);
```

The program panics, because `é` occupies bytes 3 and 4, and a slice that cuts it in half wouldn't be valid text. For the same reason, Rust doesn't let you index a string by position at all: `word[0]` is a compile error. A position in a string may fall inside a character, so "the first element" has no single meaning.

::: {.callout-warning title="Where the analogy breaks"}
R's `substr()` counts characters, so `substr(x, 1, 3)` is always the first three characters. A Rust range counts bytes and works only when you know where the characters start, as with ASCII text or a position returned by a method such as `find()`. To work character by character, loop over `chars()`.
:::

## Missing strings

An R character vector can hold `NA`:

```{r}
#| label: r-na-string
c("a", NA)
```

A Rust `String` always holds text. A string that might be missing has a different type, `Option<String>`, which @sec-missingness introduces.

::: {.callout-note title="Package developer notes: strings in compiled code" collapse="true"}
In C, each element of a character vector is a `CHARSXP`. These are read-only, and R keeps a global cache so that each distinct string is stored only once [@r-exts, sec. 5.9.8]. That's why R strings never change in place: one stored copy may be shared by many vectors.

R strings also carry an encoding and aren't always UTF-8. *Writing R Extensions* recommends `Rf_translateCharUTF8()` to get UTF-8 text from a `CHARSXP` [@r-exts, sec. 5.9.8]. Rust's `String` and `&str` must always hold valid UTF-8, so any string passed from R to Rust has to be UTF-8 first. @sec-extending-r shows how that conversion is handled.
:::

## Summary

| R | Rust |
|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| One string type, a character vector | `String` owns text; `&str` refers to it |
| Strings never change; `paste0()` builds a new one | A `mut String` can grow with `push_str()` |
| `sprintf()`, `paste0()` | `format!()` |
| `trimws()`, `toupper()`, `startsWith()` | `trim()`, `to_uppercase()`, `starts_with()` |
| `grepl()`, `gsub()`, `strsplit()` use regular expressions | `contains()`, `replace()`, `split()` match a string pattern literally |
| `strsplit()` returns a list | `split()` hands back pieces one at a time |
| String functions are vectorized | Loop over a `Vec` of strings |
| `nchar()` counts characters | `len()` counts bytes; `chars().count()` counts characters |
| `substr()` takes character positions | `&s[0..3]` takes byte positions |
| `NA_character_` | `Option<String>` |
